name: Training Datasets
blurb: Corpora used to pre-train models, with provenance and licence.

items.note: Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus; trained T5 and remains the most-downloaded classic pretraining set
15 trillion tokens of filtered CommonCrawl; the reference open web-scale pretraining corpus
The education-filtered FineWeb subset that lifted small-model benchmarks and set the quality-over-quantity pattern
The largest fully open corpus built from public-domain and permissioned text only
6TB of permissively-licensed source code behind StarCoder; gated with an opt-out process for authors
The 825GB corpus that defined open pretraining data in the GPT-Neo era; historically important, now superseded
AI2's 3-trillion-token corpus with full documentation of what went in and why; trained the OLMo models
Open reproduction of the LLaMA training mix

reading.body:
C4 remains the most-downloaded open pretraining corpus by a wide margin, with 1.3 million downloads against FineWeb's 419,000, but the gap between them reflects a transition in what practitioners expect from training data.

C4's dominance is partly historical: it trained T5 and accumulated downloads across years of use. The newer corpora tell a different story. FineWeb and its education-filtered sibling FineWeb-Edu together account for more than 800,000 downloads and represent a deliberate move toward quality filtering rather than raw scale. FineWeb-Edu specifically, noted here for lifting small-model benchmark scores, illustrates that a smaller token count with tighter curation can outperform a larger but noisier corpus. That pattern has direct compute implications: a model trained on better-filtered data can reach a target capability level with fewer training steps, which reduces the GPU-hours and therefore the power and facility costs behind a training run.

The licensing picture is mostly clean. Six of the eight corpora carry ODC-BY or are ungated, and the two exceptions, The Stack and The Pile, carry non-standard licences or a gated opt-out process rather than a blanket open licence. Common Corpus and RedPajama list no licence at all in this data, which the data notes but does not resolve. Dolma's relatively low download count despite its 3-trillion-token scale and unusually thorough provenance documentation suggests that full transparency about corpus construction has not yet become a strong selection criterion for most users. The data covers only these eight corpora and only download counts as a proxy for adoption, so it cannot speak to which datasets are used in the largest closed training runs, where compute costs are highest and data choices are least visible.
